Thanks — I’ll outline a 12-week progressive strength program suitable for a 27‑year‑old beginner training in a small flat with only a yoga mat and a doorway pull‑up bar. The plan focuses on building foundational strength, movement quality, and progressive overload using bodyweight progressions, tempo, volume, and simple conditioning. I’ll give phases, week-by-week sessions, exercise lists, sets/reps, progression notes, and brief recovery and nutrition guidance.

Key assumptions
- Healthy 27‑year‑old with no medical issues or injuries. If any pain, medical conditions, or pregnancy exist, clear with a healthcare professional first.
- Has time for 3–4 sessions per week. I’ll present a 4‑day per week option (best for strength) and a 3‑day alternative (same progress but condensed).
- Goal: increase full‑body strength (pull, push, hinge, squat, core) and work capacity.
- Equipment restrictions: bodyweight, doorway pull‑up bar, mat. Progressions use leverage, tempo, range of motion, and increased sets/reps.

Program structure overview
- Phase 1: Foundations & movement patterns (Weeks 1–4) — learn technique, build base volume, introduce progressive difficulty.
- Phase 2: Strength accumulation (Weeks 5–8) — increase intensity by adding harder progressions, increase time under tension, lower rep ranges for some sets.
- Phase 3: Strength consolidation & peak (Weeks 9–12) — focus on low‑rep maxing for bodyweight strength (e.g., full pull-ups, push‑up variants), increase single‑set intensity, and introduce testing week.

Weekly layout (4‑day plan, preferred)
- Day A: Upper Push + Horizontal Pull + Core
- Day B: Lower emphasis (squat + hinge progressions) + Conditioning
- Day C: Upper Pull + Vertical Push (press pattern via handstand practice) + Core
- Day D: Full‑body strength focus + mobility & conditioning

3‑day alternative: Combine Day A + Day B, Day C, Day D across three sessions (slightly longer sessions). I’ll note where to merge.

Progression principles
- Increase reps, sets, or difficulty of exercise progression each week. When an exercise becomes comfortably achievable at upper end of target reps, move to next progression the next week.
- Use tempo to increase difficulty: e.g., 3s eccentric (lowering), 1s pause, explosive concentric.
- Add “difficulty modifiers”: elevate feet, slow negatives, archer/uneven loading, paused reps, increase ROM.
- Rest 2–3 minutes between heavy sets, 60–90s for accessory work, 30–60s for conditioning.

Warm‑up (before every session)
- 5–8 minutes: light cardio in place (jog, high knees, jump rope imaginary), joint circles, cat–cow, hip hinges.
- Specific warm‑up set: 1–2 sets of the first exercise at easier progression (e.g., incline push‑ups on wall or knee push‑ups) 8–12 slow reps.

Phase 1 — Foundations (Weeks 1–4)
Goals: Learn movement patterns, build baseline repetitions, improve shoulder and core stability.

Week 1–2 (intro, establish baselines)
Sessions per week: 4 (or 3)
Session A (Upper Push + Horizontal Pull + Core)
- Push progression: Knee push‑ups or incline push‑ups (hands on wall/bed) — 4 sets × 8–12 reps, tempo 2s down / 0s pause / 1s up
- Horizontal pull: Australian/inverted rows using pull‑up bar at lowest safe height (or under door frame) — 4 × 6–10 reps, tempo 3s lowering
- Shoulder assistance: Bandless scapular pull‑ups (scapular retractions) or dead hang scapular shrugs — 3 × 8–10
- Core: Plank — 3 × 30–45s

Session B (Lower + Conditioning)
- Squat pattern: Slow deep bodyweight squats to a chair or box (to ensure depth) — 4 × 10–15, tempo 3s down
- Hinge pattern: Glute bridges (single or double leg progression) — 4 × 10–12
- Single‑leg assistance: Bulgarian split‑squat to box/chair (bodyweight) — 3 × 6–8 per leg
- Conditioning: 8–10 minute interval finisher: 20s high‑knees / 40s march rest × 8 rounds (or 10 rounds of 20/40)

Session C (Upper Pull + Vertical Push practice + Core)
- Pull progression: Assisted negatives for pull‑up — 4 sets × 3–6 slow negatives (3–5s descent) or band-assisted pull‑up if band exists; otherwise, door frame rows with body angle
- Vertical push prep: Pike push‑up on elevated surface (feet on bed or low box) or wall walk holds — 4 × 5–8
- Rear delt/rotator cuff: YTWL drills on mat — 3 × 8 each
- Core: Dead bug — 3 × 10–12 per side

Session D (Full body + Mobility)
- Circuit (3 rounds, rest 2 min between rounds):
  - Push: Incline push‑ups 8–10
  - Pull: Inverted rows 6–8
  - Hinge: Single‑leg glute bridge 8 per side
  - Squat: Jump squat (or slow squat) 8–10
  - Core: Hollow hold 20–30s
- Mobility focus 10 minutes: hip flexor stretch, pec doorway stretch, thoracic rotations

Week 3–4 (build volume & start progressive difficulty)
- Progressions:
  - Move knee push‑ups to full push‑ups if able for targeted reps. If full push‑ups cannot reach reps, use elevated push‑ups (hands on counter) lowering to flat push‑ups as strength improves.
  - Increase inverted row difficulty by lowering bar angle (more horizontal body).
  - Start assisted pull‑up flexed‑arm hangs and increase number of negatives per set.
  - For squats, progress toward deep unassisted bodyweight squats, tempo still controlled.
- Sets/reps: Slightly increase intensity — aim for 4–5 sets for primary movements, reps within same ranges, add one accessory set.
- Add a weekly skill block: 5–10 minutes of pull‑up practice after a session (grease the groove): 3–6 submaximal sets spread through the day.

Phase 2 — Strength accumulation (Weeks 5–8)
Goals: Increase difficulty of main lifts, shift some work to lower rep ranges with higher intensity (harder progressions), emphasize negative/eccentric control, begin aiming for unassisted pull‑up and full push‑up endurance.

General adjustments beginning Week 5:
- Replace some higher-rep sets with 5–8 rep sets for main moves; add more sets (5 sets) to keep total volume.
- Use slower tempo for eccentrics (3–4s) and 1s pause at bottom for some sets.
- Introduce unilateral loading variations to increase intensity and asymmetry control.

Weeks 5–6
Session A
- Push: Full push‑ups (or incline to flat progression) — 5 × 6–10 (3s down / explosive up)
- Horizontal pull: Inverted rows more horizontal — 5 × 6–10, add 1–2s pause at top
- Scapular pull‑ups: 4 × 8
- Core: Side plank — 3 × 30–45s per side

Session B
- Squat: Narrow (closer stance) or slow deep squats — 5 × 8–12
- Hinge: Single‑leg Romanian deadlift (bodyweight, reach to floor) — 4 × 6–8 per leg
- Split squat: Bulgarian split‑squat 4 × 8 per leg
- Conditioning: 12–15 minute AMRAP of 10 squats, 8 incline push‑ups, 6 inverted rows (pace moderate)

Session C
- Pull practice: Assisted pull‑ups aiming to reduce assistance — 5 × 3–6 negatives or 3–6 assisted reps
- Vertical push: Pike push‑ups, progress to elevated pike push‑ups — 5 × 5–8
- Rotator cuff: External rotation with towel (isometric holds) — 3 × 12
- Core: Plank with shoulder taps 3 × 20 taps

Session D
- Full body strength (5 rounds):
  - Push: Diamond or narrow push‑ups 6–8
  - Pull: Archer rows progression or one‑arm supported rows 6 per side
  - Hinge: Single‑leg bridge with pause 8 per side
  - Squat: Controlled pistol practice to a box (assisted) 4–6 per leg
  - Core: L‑sit tuck on floor or chair 4 × 10–15s

Weeks 7–8
- Further push toward unassisted pull‑up: include more frequent negative reps and short isometric holds at top (if can, do 1–2 partial unassisted reps).
- Add slow eccentrics for push‑ups (4s down) on selected sets.
- Lower sessions slightly to allow recovery if intensity increases: keep 4 sessions per week but monitor fatigue.

Session sample changes:
- If client can do 1–3 full pull‑ups by Week 7, program sets like: 5 sets of 2–4 total reps (assisted to reach target), plus 2 negatives per set.
- For push: Incorporate deficit push‑ups (hands on elevated surface to increase range) or weighted backpack if available later (optional).

Phase 3 — Strength consolidation & peak (Weeks 9–12)
Goals: Convert accumulated volume into maximal strength — aim for multiple unassisted pull‑ups, confident full push‑ups, improved pistol squat ability. Lower rep ranges for primary moves, include testing.

Weeks 9–10
- Emphasize harder progressions; reduce reps to 4–6 for main lifts, increase sets 5–6.
- Introduce paused reps at bottom and explosive concentric to train power.

Sample Session A (Week 9)
- Push: Decline or feet-elevated push‑ups (feet on chair) — 6 sets × 4–6 reps (3s eccentric, pause, explosive up)
- Pull: Pull‑up progression — 6 sets × 2–4 reps (assisted if needed), include 2s top hold every 2nd set
- Horizontal pull accessory: Slow inverted rows 4 × 6–8
- Core: Weighted (backpack) plank or extended plank 3 × 45–60s if ready

Session B

Below is a practical, progressive at‑home cardio plan your client can do in the flat (no equipment), integrated into the 12‑week strength program. It includes types of cardio, weekly structure options (beginner and more advanced), specific workouts (HIIT, steady‑state, low‑impact), progressions, pacing cues, and how to combine cardio with the strength plan so it supports — not hinders — strength gains.

Key principles
- Make cardio short and targeted so it improves conditioning and recovery without interfering with strength gains. Prioritise strength sessions; place cardio on separate days or after strength work (light cardio) when possible.
- Use a mix of low‑impact steady state (LISS), higher‑intensity interval training (HIIT), and mobility/active recovery.
- Begin conservatively — 2–3 cardio sessions/week, then adjust based on recovery and goals. As a beginner aiming to build strength, keep total weekly cardio to ~75–150 minutes, leaning lower in the early weeks.

Weekly cardio structure options
- Minimal (recommended for most beginners): 2 sessions/week
  - 1 LISS session (20–30 minutes)
  - 1 HIIT or tempo session (10–15 minutes)
- Moderate (if he wants more conditioning): 3 sessions/week
  - 1 LISS (30–40 min)
  - 1 HIIT (10–15 min)
  - 1 low‑impact conditioning or mobility (20 min)
- Higher (only if recovery is excellent and strength is still progressing): 3–4 sessions/week, but reduce volume or intensity if strength stalls.

How to place cardio around strength workouts
- Preferably on non‑strength days, or after strength sessions (not before heavy strength work) so glycolytic fatigue doesn't reduce lifting performance.
- Example weekly placement (4 strength days): LISS on Day after Session B, HIIT on an off day between Session C and D, active recovery on a light day or rest day.
- If short HIIT must be same day as strength, do strength first, wait 30–60 minutes, then HIIT.

Cardio modalities suitable for a small flat (no equipment)
- Low‑impact: brisk walking in place, marching, step‑ups on a sturdy step or bottom stair, cycling substitute (seated high‑knees march), shadow boxing.
- No‑impact/high‑intensity: jump rope (if ceiling height allows and downstairs neighbors not an issue), burpees, mountain climbers, jumping jacks, squat jumps, tuck jumps (use impact sparingly).
- Mixed/functional circuits: bodyweight circuits combining cardio and strength moves (e.g., AMRAP style or timed rounds).
- Stair climbing (if building access allows walking stairs instead of in‑flat jumping) — great low‑impact conditioning.

Specific cardio workouts (doable in a small flat)

LISS (Low‑Intensity Steady State)
- Purpose: build aerobic base, assist recovery, burn calories, low interference with strength.
- Duration: 20–40 minutes
- Pace: conversational, 50–65% of max heart rate (easy breathing).
- Examples:
  - Walk in place with dynamic arm swings, alternating high knees at low intensity.
  - Continuous step‑ups on a single step or sturdy stair at steady pace.
  - Shadow boxing with light footwork and movement.
- Progression: increase time by 5–10 minutes every 2 weeks or increase tempo slightly.

HIIT options (short, high intensity — more metabolic)
- Purpose: improve anaerobic capacity and conditioning; keep brief to limit interference with strength.
- Safe beginner HIIT template: 10–15 minutes total (including 1–2 minute warm‑up)
- Example A — 10‑minute Tabata style (you can scale reps)
  - Warm‑up: 2 min brisk march/light jogging in place
  - Tabata rounds: 20s on (max effort), 10s off — repeat 8 rounds (4 min) with 1 min easy between two blocks if repeating
  - Exercises: burpees, mountain climbers, squat jumps, alternating between exercises for each 20s work.
  - Cool‑down: 2–3 min walk and stretch
- Example B — 12‑minute EMOM (Every Minute On the Minute)
  - Warm‑up: 2–3 min
  - Minute 1: 30s high knees, 30s rest
  - Minute 2: 30s burpees or half‑burpees, 30s rest
  - Minute 3: 30s mountain climbers, 30s rest
  - Repeat for 3–4 rounds (9–12 min)
- Progression: increase rounds, reduce rest, or substitute harder movements (full burpees → burpee tuck jumps).

Low‑impact HIIT (if ceiling/noise concern)
- Example 10‑minute session:
  - Warm‑up: 2 min march
  - 40s effort / 20s rest × 6 rounds:
    - Round pattern: fast step‑ups, fast bodyweight squats (no jump), fast plank jacks (march plank if needed)
  - Cool‑down 2 min

Circuit‑style cardio (combined conditioning)
- 15–20 minute AMRAP (as many rounds as possible)
  - 10 bodyweight squats
  - 8 incline push‑ups
  - 6 inverted rows
  - 10 mountain climbers (each side counts as 1)
  - Pace is steady; this improves both conditioning and work capacity.

  - Warm‑up 2–3 minutes walking
  - 30s up fast, walk down easy (repeat 8–10 times)
  - Cool‑down walk 2 min

Progression plan across 12 weeks

2) Adjustable weighted backpack (or a small weighted vest)
- What to buy: Strong backpack (hiking style) and a few sandbags, weight plates, or heavy books/weights to load it; or a low‑cost adjustable weighted vest (10–40 lb / 5–20 kg capacity).
- Why: Simple way to add axial load for squats, lunges, push‑ups, pull‑ups (wearing during negatives/assisted sets), bridges, and carries. Much cheaper and more space‑efficient than plates/dumbbells.
- How to use: Add progressive weight (start +5–10 kg depending on ability) to push‑up sets, squats, and belt‑squat style work. Always secure load so it doesn’t shift.

- How to use: Continue strict pull‑ups, add negatives with vest, isometric holds, and hanging leg raises.

4) Pair of adjustable dumbbells or kettlebell(s)
- What to buy: If space and budget allow, adjustable dumbbells (e.g., 2.5–25 kg / 5–55 lb per dumbbell) or a couple of kettlebells (8–16 kg / 18–35 lb to start).

5) Pair of parallettes or push‑up bars (or sturdy low boxes)
- What to buy: Lightweight parallettes or stable push‑up handles / low plyo box.
- Why: Increase push‑up ROM, practice L‑sit, planche lean progressions, and dips (if parallettes tall enough). Easier on wrists; low profile and stackable.
- How to use: Elevated hand positions for deeper push‑ups, L‑sit holds, tuck planche work, and wrist-friendly pressing.

Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8) — Push intensity prescription

Overall goal
- Increase mechanical tension and neuromuscular stress on push muscles while still allowing recovery for the rest of the program. Shift from higher‑rep accumulation to moderate reps with slightly higher intensity and slower eccentrics to build strength and control.

Weekly structure for push work
- Primary push sessions appear twice per week across the 4‑day split (Day A and Day D/full‑body). Treat one session as “heavy strength focus” and the other as “volume/skill & accessory.”
- Heavy push session: lower reps, more sets, higher RPE (but not maximal every set).
- Volume session: higher total reps, skill work (e.g., handstand/pike practice), and accessory triceps/shoulder work.

Intensity targets (sets/reps/tempo/RPE)
- Heavy push (strength) session
  - Exercise examples: full push‑ups → feet‑elevated push‑ups → deficit/eccentric emphases → weighted backpack push‑ups
  - Sets: 5 sets per main push exercise
  - Reps: 4–6 reps per set (or 6–8 if client can't reach lower range yet; prioritize progression)
  - Tempo: 3–4s eccentric (slow lowering), 1s pause at bottom on the last 1–2 sets of a movement, explosive concentric
  - Rest: 2.5–3.5 minutes between heavy sets
  - Target RPE: 7–8 for most sets, 8–9 for the final set of each exercise
  - Notes: If client can do more than 8 reps easily, progress to a harder variation. Use slow negatives and paused reps if assistance still required.

- Volume/skill session
  - Exercise examples: higher‑rep push‑ups, incline/decline work, archer push‑up progressions, pike push‑ups for shoulder emphasis
  - Sets: 4–5 sets for primary movement, 3–4 for accessory
  - Reps: 8–15 per set depending on variation (aim total weekly volume for push chest/tris ~30–60 hard reps across sessions)
  - Tempo: 2–3s eccentric, controlled concentric; incorporate some explosive reps for 1–2 sets
  - Rest: 60–90s between sets for higher rep sets, 90–120s for heavier accessories
  - Target RPE: 6–8 (submaximal, focus on volume and form)

Progression options (how to make push work harder)
- Decrease assistance / increase leverage:
  - Knee → incline → full → feet‑elevated → decline/deficit → archer → one‑arm assisted
- Manipulate tempo:
  - Slow eccentrics (3–5s) and pause holds at bottom (1–2s) increase time‑under‑tension and strength gains.

Below is a practical mobility routine tailored to your 27‑year‑old beginner client training in a small flat. It’s designed to support the 12‑week strength program, improve movement quality for push/pull/squat/hinge patterns, reduce injury risk, and help recovery. It requires only a mat, wall, and doorway (for pec stretch), plus the pull‑up bar if available.

How to use this routine
- Frequency: Daily short routine (8–12 minutes) and a longer session (20–25 minutes) 2× per week.
- Timing: Daily routine can be done in the morning, after workouts as cooldown, or on off days. Longer sessions best on rest or light days, or after an easy LISS walk.
- Intensity: Gentle, breathe through movements. Mobility is about range and control, not pain. If anything hurts sharply, stop and regress.
- Progression: Increase range of motion, hold times, and add a few controlled repetitions as movement improves.

Daily quick routine (8–12 minutes) — do this most days
1) General warm‑up (1–2 min)
- March or light in‑place movement 60–90s (swing arms, gentle hip hinge, ankle circles) to raise body temp slightly.

2) Thoracic rotation with reach (90–120s)
- Kneel on mat or stand. Place one hand behind head, other hand on floor or knee. Rotate the upper torso to bring elbow toward ceiling; open chest. 8–10 slow reps per side.
- Purpose: improve thoracic extension/rotation for better push/pull posture and handstand practice.

3) Banded or doorway pec stretch (90s total)
- If doorway: place forearm on doorframe at 90° elbow height, gently rotate torso away until a stretch is felt across chest. Hold 30–45s each side.
- If no doorway: clasp hands behind back and lift gently while keeping chest tall. Hold 30–45s.
- Purpose: open chest, aid shoulder overhead mobility.

4) Shoulder dislocates / band pull‑aparts alternative (60–90s)
- Use a loop band or towel: hold wide, raise overhead and behind down to hips (or do band pull‑aparts: 3 sets × 10–15). If no band, use a towel.
- Slow and controlled, 8–12 reps.
- Purpose: shoulder girdle mobility and scapular control.

5) Hip flexor + quad stretch (1–2 min per side)
- Low lunge: one knee on mat, other foot forward. Tuck pelvis under and squeeze glute of back leg to feel front hip stretch. Optional: reach up overhead to increase torso extension. Hold 40–60s each side.
- Purpose: relieve anterior hip tightness from sitting; improves squat depth and pelvic position.

6) 90/90 hip rotation (1–2 min)
- Sit on mat: lead leg in front at 90°, trail leg to side at 90°. Lean forward over front leg then upright, then do small rotations. 8–10 reps then switch sides.
- Purpose: internal/external hip rotation and squat/pistol preparation.

7) Hamstring and calf active stretch (90s)
- Standing hamstring reach: hinge at hips with slight knee bend, reach toward toes, then perform a calf raise and dorsiflex stretch. 10 slow reps.
- Lying single‑leg hamstring active flex: loop towel around foot, actively pull toes toward you and flex/point 8–10 reps per side.
- Purpose: prepare hinge and squat mechanics.

8) Ankle dorsiflexion drills (60s)
- Toe‑elevated calf stretch: stand with toes on a small rolled towel or book, shift knee forward over toes (bodyweight) 10 reps each side. Or kneeling ankle mobilization: lean forward with foot flat. 8–10 reps.
- Purpose: improve squat depth and knee travel.

9) Cat–cow + child's pose breathing cooldown (60–90s)
- 30–45s cat–cow flow, then 30–45s child's pose breathing.
- Purpose: spinal mobility and relaxation.

Longer mobility session (20–25 minutes) — 2× per week
Do this session on a rest or light day. Hold stretches longer, add more controlled strength‑mobility.

1) 3–5 minute light aerobic warm‑up
- March in place, hip circles, arm swings.

2) Foam‑roll/self‑massage alternatives (if no foam roller, use a rolled towel) (3–4 min)
- Quads, glutes, lats, thoracic spine roll (1 min each targeted area).

3) Thoracic extension work (3–4 min)
- 2 sets of 8–10 reps of thoracic extensions over a rolled towel or on a chair (hands behind head, open chest).
- 2 sets of 5–8 wall slides: stand with back vs wall, arms in W then slide up to Y keeping contact.

4) Shoulder mobility + stability (3–4 min)
- 3 sets of 8 band pull‑aparts (or towel pull‑aparts)
- 3 sets of 6–8 scapular pull‑ups or scapular retractions (on pull‑up bar) — slow.

5) Hip capsule + glute activation (4–5 min)
- Couch stretch variation or 90/90 holds: 2 × 45–60s each side.
- Glute activation: 2 × 12‑15 banded glute bridges or single‑leg bridges (if no band, bodyweight).

6) Deep squat hold + ankle mobile work (3–4 min)
- 3 sets of 30–45s deep squat hold (use wall/door frame support if needed). Between holds, perform ankle mobilizations: 8 reps per side pressing knee forward.
- Purpose: reinforce upright torso and ankle mobility for squat depth.

7) Pigeon / figure‑4 for external hip rotation (2–3 min)
- 2 × 45s per side (can be done lying on back with figure‑4 if floor tightness restricts seated position).

8) Core & posterior chain integration (2–3 min)

Other Phase 2 session templates
Day A (example heavy push day)

- Mobility

Day B (lower focus)

- Mobility

Push intensity prescription (specific)
- Heavy push session (strength-focused)
  - Main push: 5 sets × 4–6 reps (or 6–8 if client cannot lower yet)
  - Tempo: 3–4s eccentric, 1s pause at bottom on some sets, explosive concentric
  - Rest: 2.5–3.5 minutes between heavy sets
  - RPE target: 7–8 most sets, 8–9 on final set
  - Accessory: Narrow/diamond push‑ups 3 × 6–8; triceps band extensions 3 × 10–12
- Volume/skill push day
  - Main push: 4–5 sets × 8–12 reps (tempo 2–3s eccentric)
  - Skill: pike/handstand practice, archer push‑up progressions
  - Accessory: face pulls / YTWL 3 × 10–12

How to progress week‑to‑week (quick guide)
- Week 1–2: establish baseline and technique
- Week 3–4: increase volume/sets or move to harder progression
- Week 5–8: increase intensity — use Phase 2 push prescription (heavy & volume days); add bands/backpack as available
- Week 9–10: reduce reps/increase sets for strength (4–6 reps main lifts)

- Week 12: testing — evaluate pull‑ups, push‑ups, pistol strength

Auto‑regulation and recovery rules
- If a primary set drops >2 reps below target or RPE consistently >9, reduce load/progression or add an extra recovery day.
- Sleep: aim 7–9 hours. Hydration 2–3 L/day.
- Reduce cardio if strength deteriorates or soreness increases.

Testing metrics at end of program (Week 12)

- Max consecutive full push‑ups
- Max single‑leg pistol reps each side to a standard box/height
